analysis.one_liner: Lets the consumer product safety agency publicize hazards without manufacturers blocking it, and raises fines.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a vote: introduced with 15 Democratic cosponsors, it sat in the House Energy and Commerce Committee until the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Under current law, a manufacturer can go to court to stop the Consumer Product Safety Commission from publicly revealing information it submits about its own products, including safety warnings and hazards. This bill would take away that ability, so the agency could disclose product-safety information without a company being able to block it. It would also raise the top fine for violating product safety law from $15 million to $50 million. The bill never advanced past its committee referral.
analysis.who_benefits: Consumers, who would learn about hazards in products they buy — including products for children and the home — sooner and more completely, because manufacturers could no longer sue to keep the safety agency from disclosing information about those hazards. The higher fine cap also gives the agency more leverage against companies that violate safety rules.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Consumers and families buying everyday products

how_it_helps.text: The bill repeals the part of the Consumer Product Safety Act (Section 6(b)) that lets a manufacturer file a claim to block the Commission from publicly disclosing product information, such as safety warnings [S2] [S3].
It raises the maximum civil penalty for consumer product safety violations from $15 million to $50 million, applying to violations occurring on or after enactment [S2] [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Consumer product manufacturers, who would lose their ability to keep the safety agency from publicly disclosing information about their products, and would face a higher ceiling on fines for violations. Some of those costs could show up in prices, and companies might share less information with the agency voluntarily if they fear immediate public disclosure.

drawbacks.text: Manufacturers have long argued that Section 6(b)'s confidentiality protections are what make them willing to share candid, early information with the Commission; without the ability to prevent disclosure, companies might withhold or delay reporting hazards, which could slow recalls [S2].
Raising the maximum penalty to $50 million raises compliance and litigation costs for product makers, costs that small manufacturers may feel more sharply than large ones [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefit — the public learning about dangerous products from the agency charged with protecting them, without a company being able to sue to keep it quiet — is substantial and directly serves people who buy those products. The main good-faith objection, that removing confidentiality might make companies less forthcoming with the agency, is real but secondary: the same information the public currently cannot see is exactly what companies use to block disclosure, and the agency can still use confidential channels for coordination while making hazard warnings public. The penalty increase is modest relative to the revenue of large product makers. On balance the bill's benefits to consumers outweigh its costs.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee, which never took it up, and it died when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Bobby Rush introduced the bill on January 9, 2020, and it was referred the same day to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce [S1] [S5].
Fifteen House Democrats cosponsored it; no Republicans did [S4].
The action history shows no further steps — no markup, no hearing on record, no floor vote — after the referral [S5].

The bill would have repealed the provision of the Consumer Product Safety Act that lets manufacturers enjoin (legally block) the Commission's public disclosure of product information, and raised the maximum civil penalty from $15 million to $50 million [S2] [S3].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Consumer product manufacturers are better off: they keep their ability to block the safety agency from publicly disclosing information about their products, and the ceiling on fines for safety violations stays at $15 million.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Product makers who could still block disclosure

sides.party_line_note: The bill's sponsor and all 15 cosponsors were Democrats; no Republicans signed on, and the bill never reached a floor vote where party splits could be measured.

industries.note: The bill would strip manufacturers of their power to sue to stop the Consumer Product Safety Commission from publicly disclosing information about their products' hazards, and would raise the top fine for safety violations from $15 million to $50 million. That disclosure power is what lets companies keep hazards they report to the agency out of public view, so its loss cuts directly against the industry's interest and for consumers.
The agency would gain the ability to warn the public about product hazards without first litigating against the companies involved, and a higher penalty cap strengthens its enforcement hand.
